rationale: The book's core identification of works as deeds (not a synonym for obedience) that become obedience or disobedience according to the governing lawgiver is the minimum claim that diverges from the common fruit/evidence reading, and the supplied texts establish it more tightly than the broader common alternative. Exodus 18:20 places 'the work that they must do' in parallel with ordinances, laws, and the way to walk, defining the term as the deed itself; Micah 6:16 shows the same term for the deeds of Ahab under rival statutes; Romans 4:4-5 and Luke 17:7-10 isolate wage-claiming labor from duty-obedience; James 2:21-22 shows Abraham's deed as faith made visible. The common view correctly registers that works are deeds and often evidence faith or flesh, but it regularly collapses 'works' into 'obedience' or 'meritorious fruit' without the lawgiver distinction the cited passages require. The book's secondary elaborations (Romans wage-debt, James faith-perfecting, unprofitable servants) follow directly from those texts and introduce no unsupported steps. No counter accounts for the same definitional and contrastive details with fewer assumptions.
book_core_identification: Works are deeds—not a synonym for obedience. A work becomes obedience when it executes God's command, or disobedience when another lawgiver governs it.
book_secondary_elaborations: Romans 4 uses the laborer's work offered for wages and debt
James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible
Complete obedience still earns no wage: the servant has only done his duty (Luke 17:7-10)
strongest_counter_interpretation: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'works' are understood as the outward deeds or actions of a person that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition—good works being the visible fruit of genuine faith, God's grace, and a regenerated heart, and evil works being the visible fruit of unbelief, the sinful nature ('the flesh'), or alignment with darkness. Works function as evidence or fruit rather than as the root: they reveal what a person truly is (a tree known by its fruit), and they will be the basis of divine assessment at judgment because they manifest the heart.
counter_core_identification: Works as outward deeds that evidence the inner spiritual condition (good works as fruit of faith/grace; evil works as fruit of flesh/unbelief)
material_core_denial: None; the counter agrees that works are deeds and can be good or evil, but it does not isolate the non-synonymy with obedience or the governing-lawgiver criterion that the book treats as definitional.
counter_case: Ephesians 2:8-10 frames good works as the purpose for which the already-saved are created, not the root of salvation
James 2:14-26 and Matthew 7:16-20 treat works as the necessary fruit/evidence that living faith produces
Revelation 20:12-13 and Romans 2:6 base final judgment on works as the public manifestation of the heart
Galatians 5:19-23 and John 3:19-21 contrast works of the flesh/darkness with works wrought in God as indicators of spiritual parentage
book_explanatory_advantages: Exodus 18:20 supplies an explicit definitional parallel (ordinances + way to walk + work to do) that the common fruit reading never cites
Micah 6:16 uses the identical term for the deeds of Ahab under rival statutes, confirming the lawgiver criterion
Luke 17:7-10 + Romans 4:4-5 together separate complete duty-obedience from wage-claiming labor without collapsing either into 'fruit'
James 2:21-22 is read as faith enacted by a deed, not as evidence that redefines the term 'works' itself
The distinction keeps 'works of the law' and faith-works as the same class of deeds under different masters, avoiding an ad-hoc semantic split
counter_explanatory_advantages: Unifies the majority of New Testament occurrences under a single fruit/evidence paradigm that matches tree-fruit, light-darkness, and judgment imagery
Explains the soteriological 'not of works' texts (Eph 2, Rom 3-4, Gal 2) as excluding meritorious root while still requiring fruit
Accounts for the repeated evaluation of churches and persons by their works (Rev 2-3, Matt 25) as public disclosure of allegiance
unresolved_objections: The entry and chapter do not systematically treat Johannine uses of Jesus' 'works' as signs/miracles or every instance of 'works of the law' in the New Perspective debates
Some secondary elaborations (faith made visible, no wage for duty) already appear in standard Protestant expositions of the same texts
